requirement:
# REQ-2297: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2297

#### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.
MessagePack generated code is not decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.

Because it is very hard to write good coverage for generated MessagePack code, it may skew coverage numbers, especially on large projects with a lot of generated code.

#### Describe the solution you'd like
I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.  I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too.

#### Describe alternatives you've considered
There are no alternatives, it is close to impossible to write good coverage for generated code as it covers many edge cases.

#### Additional context

N/A

story.summary: The source generator templates (resolver, composite resolver, object formatter, string-key formatter, enum formatter, union formatter) now put `[global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on every emitted type, including the nested `FormatterCache<T>` and `GetFormatterHelper` classes. Each attribute is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. A small change in TransformUtilities makes the nesting brace end with a line break, so the `#if` always starts on its own line. 222 snapshot files were regenerated. A README paragraph and a new test class with two tests were added.
story.why: Issue 2297 asks for all generated MessagePack code to carry ExcludeFromCodeCoverage so that it does not skew coverage numbers.
touches_beyond_requirement: TransformUtilities.EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces now emits `{\r\n` instead of `{` when type constraints exist. Without it, an emitted `#if` could land mid-line. It changes the whitespace of generated output for constrained nesting types.
README gains a paragraph. Its second sentence (all target frameworks, including netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework) contradicts the code's `#if` guard.
The attribute is deliberately left out for netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework consumers. The issue asked for 'all generated code', so this is a narrower delivery than requested.
story.confidence_overview: High that every template emits the guarded attribute: the template and .cs pairs match (S1) and the snapshots change uniformly (S2). Medium on whether the guard is right. ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists in .NET Framework 4.0+ and netstandard2.0, so the guard looks unnecessary and leaves those users unserved. Low on the README, which is factually wrong about this code. The new tests only check text substrings per file and do not compile the output.

findings.description: The README says the attribute is emitted for every target framework, including netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework. The templates do the opposite: they wrap it in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. The documentation is false.

The guard appears unnecessary. System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists in .NET Framework 4.0+ and netstandard2.0, where it can be applied to classes. Consumers on those targets (common for libraries and Unity) still get generated code counted in coverage, which is the problem the issue raised. The test comment at CodeCoverageExclusionTests.cs line 18 repeats the incorrect rationale.

The attribute is placed on `partial class <Resolver>`, and the user declares the other half of that class. ExcludeFromCodeCoverage has AllowMultiple=false.
